title_original: Dimakatso Mathopa Lays the Colonial Gaze to Rest
excerpt_original: The South African photographer stages herself in cyanotype, a nineteenth-century process, to take back the role colonial imagery assigns to Black women. She lends her own features to her grandmother, the sole keeper of a story about land. L’article Dimakatso Mathopa Lays the…

blocks.text: Photography turns two hundred this year. The Voices sector at Paris Photo answers with a theme, “The Disappearance,” entrusted to Zasha Colah and Francesco Zanot: it invites us to “rethink this anniversary as a threshold: between commemoration and obsolescence, between mourning and renewal.” In the nave of the Grand Palais, Afronova Gallery, out of Johannesburg, shows Dimakatso Mathopa’s latest work.

Colonial imagery long assigned Black women two parts: the maid and the ethnographic specimen. Émilie Demon, who heads Afronova, frames the artist’s project: she explores “how the colonial gaze has subverted their representation today.” Since 2017, the ongoing series “Individual Beings Relocated” has taken that role and handed it to its author. Dimakatso Mathopa inhabits her own pictures, and she inhabits them as the owner.

Born in 1995 in Mpumalanga, the artist studied printmaking at the University of Johannesburg. Silkscreen and Van Dyke brown led her to the cyanotype, an 1842 process long given over to taking inventory of the world. You sensitize cotton paper with two iron salts, you set it in the sun, and a Prussian blue rises to the surface.

The idea began in a conversation, opened after her mother’s death. “My grandfather was a traditional healer and he was well known in the area of the Free State, so they were gifted land by one of the white men that really admired my grandfather,” Dimakatso Mathopa says. A sangoma heals bodies and consults the ancestors. Her grandfather practiced in Viljoenskroon, a small farming town.

The gift came on the eve of apartheid’s end, as white owners sold off their property. The family moved into the master’s house and stayed three years. Mahogany and silver remained foreign to her grandmother. “She was very much uncomfortable in the space,” the artist recalls. The old woman polished the floors day after day, to justify the presence of a Black woman beneath those ceilings.

In 2017, Dimakatso Mathopa moved into a Victorian house in Johannesburg, the Lindfield Victorian House Museum, in Auckland Park. The house dates from 1910 and keeps its original furniture. Its owner still lives there among the curios. “Based on my grandmother’s memory, I decided to find a space that imitates the memory of my grandmother,” the artist explains. Beeswax polish thickens the air.

In one of the rooms she found a period undergarment and slipped it against her skin. She stood at the mirror, half naked, and took the part of the matriarch. “I wore it to create that moment of my grandmother being intimately in the space,” she says. She played her mother as well, who had passed through these same rooms.

To soften the cyanotype’s blue, the artist reaches into the kitchen. “I use black tea and bleach to tone it,” she says. Black tea was her grandmother’s drink. The bleach came from the bucket she took to the floors. The prints slide toward the sepia of old photographs.

She then brought those prints to her grandmother. “I showed her the images and we both selected the ones I was going to work with,” she says. The old woman died soon after that sorting. Her great-aunt then led Dimakatso Mathopa to the house in the Free State. The family sold it when her grandfather died, and another family lives there now.

Dimakatso Mathopa also paints in acrylic on acetate, a transparent sheet the light passes through, and gathers these recent works under the title “Individual Beings (Moving)”. Through that transparency the body appears clothed, and the hung work lays a shadow on the wall. The artist calls herself spiritual and says she has received a calling. Her own dead return in that shadow. The colonial gaze leaves the room. The artist leaves too, her grandmother beside her: “She acts as a shadow whenever I create the work.”

“Individual Beings,” Afronova Gallery , booth B58, Voices sector, Paris Photo , Grand Palais, Paris, through November 15, 2026. A finalist for the Norval Sovereign African Art Prize and the first recipient of the Elaine Harris Grant, Dimakatso Mathopa showed a new body of work in Paris this past March, “They Tried To Bury Us, They Didn’t Know I Was The Seed,” curated by Laura Serani.
